title: Critique of Agent Model: Agentic vs. Agentive Systems
hook: When is a system really an 'agent' and not just a clever workflow? This paper draws the line at whether agency is internalized or scaffolded — and sketches an architecture for the former.
key_points: Argues we need to clarify where automation ends and genuine agency begins — both to build capable systems and to reason about risk.
Analyzes agent architectures along five dimensions: goal, identity, decision-making, self-regulation, and learning.
Distinguishes agentic systems (competence lives in engineered, external scaffolding) from agentive systems (capabilities arise endogenously, internalized).
Genuine agency, the authors argue, requires these structures to be internalized within the system, not assembled by external orchestration.
Proposes a Goal-Identity-Configurator (GIC) architecture: hierarchical goals, identity evolution, world-model-grounded reasoning, learned self-regulation, and self-directed learning.
content_html: The word "agent" now stretches from coding assistants to existential-risk scenarios, often in the same breath. Critique of Agent Model steps back to ask what agency actually means — and where automation stops and genuine autonomy begins.
extra_html:
Drawing the line

Borrowing from Descartes' grounding of agency in independent thought (and from how science fiction portrays autonomous beings), the authors survey today's AI agents and analyze their architectures along five dimensions: goal, identity, decision-making, self-regulation, and learning. Their key distinction: agentic systems, whose competence is assembled through engineered external scaffolding, versus agentive systems, whose capabilities — including social interaction — arise endogenously. Genuine agency, they argue, requires these structures to be internalized within the system rather than bolted on from outside.

A proposed architecture

Building on that, they sketch a Goal-Identity-Configurator (GIC) architecture for a general-purpose agent: hierarchical goal decomposition, identity evolution, simulative reasoning grounded in a separately trained world model, learned self-regulation, and self-directed learning from real and simulated experience. The framing doubles as a lens on safety — more autonomous "agentive" systems raise sharper questions of auditability and control, even when kept under human oversight. The full argument is in the paper, linked as the source.

related.title: World Models Meet Language Models
related.hook: A world model can imagine what happens next; an LLM can reason about it. The hard part is knowing when to trust the daydream — and when the simulation is just plausible nonsense.

related.title: Agentic Environment Engineering: A Survey
related.hook: Agents only get as good as the worlds they practice in. This survey maps the full lifecycle of agent environments — how we model, synthesize, evaluate, and grow them.

flashcards.prompt: How does the paper distinguish 'agentic' from 'agentive' systems?

choices.text: Agentic systems get competence from engineered external scaffolding; agentive systems have capabilities that arise endogenously, internalized within the system
Agentic systems are larger models; agentive ones are smaller
Agentic systems use tools; agentive ones never use tools

flashcards.explanation_html: The boundary is where competence lives: in the surrounding workflow (agentic) versus inside the system itself (agentive) — the latter being the authors' bar for genuine autonomy.
